Team NazarX · Orbita 2026 · schematic rev C · 24 Oct 2026

SnailPulse, part by part

SnailPulse listens for a garden snail's heartbeat through its shell during a stratospheric flight. Rev C is the heartbeat-only board: an infrared sensor, a two-stage analog filter and amplifier, a 1.65 V reference, and the connectors that tie it to the IntroSat flight controller and three I²C sensors.

Every picture below is cut from the current KiCad file (the version saved this evening). Click a stage or a part name and it lights up on the schematic.

Updated 29 Oct: a DHT-11 (on PC6) and an MQ-7 (on PB1) were added on J6 pins 3 and 2. Updated 30 Oct: there are now two snails. Snail 1 wears the TCRT5000 (amplifier → PB0), snail 2 the MAX30100 on J9 (I²C, 0x57); each gets its own heart rate. The second BMP280 planned on 29 Oct was dropped: only J8's BMP280 (0x76) stays. The text below says so; the schematic pictures don't show it yet. New sensors → · Checks and which code to upload →

A1 IR light into the shell→ A2 light → voltage→ A3 remove DC→ A4 amplify ×101→ A5 cut fast noise→ A6 into the ADC→ A7 firmware counts beats→ C out over J6
A

Heartbeat sensor and amplifier

The heart sits just under the shell. Each beat changes how much infrared light bounces back to the sensor by roughly 0.1–1 %. Everything in this block exists to find that tiny change, make it about a hundred times bigger, and throw everything else away before it reaches the STM32's pin PB0.

A1

Shine infrared light into the shell

The TCRT5000 is two parts in one plastic package: an infrared LED (950 nm, invisible to us) and a phototransistor facing the same way. Pressed against the shell over the heart, the LED lights up the tissue and the phototransistor catches what reflects back. When the heart contracts and fills, the amount of reflected light changes slightly.

  • The sensor itself. It lives on the snail at the end of the J1 cable, not on the board, so it is marked "exclude from board" in KiCad.
  • Sets the LED current. An LED drops an almost fixed voltage (about 1.25 V), so without a resistor nothing would limit the current and the LED would burn out.
I_LED = (5 V − 1.25 V) / 220 Ω ≈ 17 mA (datasheet max 60 mA → ~30 %) P_R1 = 0.017² × 220 Ω ≈ 64 mW (a ¼ W resistor is fine)

Why 5 V for the LEDFrom 3.3 V the same resistor gives (3.3 − 1.25) / 220 ≈ 9 mA: half the light and a weaker heartbeat signal.

If it's wrong: too much current heats the LED right next to the snail; too little and the pulse sinks into noise.

A2

Turn reflected light into a voltage

Light landing on the phototransistor lets current flow from its collector (on +3.3 V) to its emitter. More light, more current. That current then flows through RV3 to ground, and Ohm's law turns it into a voltage on the net SENSE.

  • The phototransistor half. It behaves like a current source controlled by light.
  • A trimmer wired as a variable resistor (wiper tied to one end). It sets the sensitivity: more resistance means more volts for the same light. You turn it so SENSE rests near 1 V with the sensor on the snail.
V_SENSE = I_photo × R_RV3 example: 50 µA × 20 kΩ = 1.0 V ceiling: 3.3 V − V_CE(sat) ≈ 2.9 V (so the next stage is never overdriven)
SENSE on the full 0–3.3 V scale: a flat line near 1 V. The heartbeat is in there, about 2 mV tall, far too small to see. (Illustrative.)

Why aim for 1 VIt's mid-range, so the signal has room to move both ways. Near 0 V the transistor is starved of light; near 2.9 V it saturates and flattens the pulse.

If it's wrong: RV3 at maximum with a bright reflection pins SENSE at ~2.9 V (no pulse). RV3 near zero keeps SENSE near 0 V.

A3

Remove the DC and re-centre at 1.65 V

This is a high-pass filter. C11 passes changes but blocks a steady voltage. R15 ties the far side of C11 to VREF (1.65 V). After this stage the signal is the heartbeat ripple sitting on 1.65 V instead of on 1 V, and it goes into U2A's + input (pin 3).

  • Blocks the ~1 V resting level and lets the beat-to-beat change through.
  • Gives the op-amp input a DC path to VREF (an op-amp input must never float) and, together with C11, sets the cut-off frequency.
f_c = 1 / (2π · R15 · C11) = 1 / (2π · 1 MΩ · 1 µF) = 0.16 Hz ≈ 9.5 bpm τ = R15 · C11 = 1 s → settles in ~5 s after power-up or a bump
U2A pin 3, zoomed to an 8 mV window: now centred on 1.65 V, and the beats are visible. Small fast wiggles are noise. (Illustrative, 30 bpm.)

Why we need itThe 1 V resting level is hundreds of times bigger than the pulse. Amplify it ×101 and the output would slam into the 3.3 V rail and stay there. Why 1 MΩ is safe: the MCP6002 is a CMOS op-amp with ~1 pA input current, which makes only 1 µV across 1 MΩ.

If it's wrong: a higher cut-off (say 1 Hz) would start eating slow heartbeats, and a cold snail's heart can drop toward 10 bpm.

A4

Amplify it 101 times

U2A is a non-inverting amplifier. The trick is that R16 goes to VREF, not to ground, so the gain only applies to how far the input is from 1.65 V. 1.65 V in gives 1.65 V out; 1.65 V + 2 mV in gives 1.65 V + 0.2 V out.

  • Half A of the dual op-amp (pins 1, 2, 3). Rail-to-rail CMOS on 3.3 V, so its output can swing almost the full 0–3.3 V ADC range. 1 MHz gain-bandwidth, so at gain 101 it stays flat to ~10 kHz, far above any heartbeat.
  • Feedback resistor from the output back to the − input.
  • From the − input to VREF. The R17/R16 ratio sets the gain.
G = 1 + R17 / R16 = 1 + 100k / 1k = 101 (20·log₁₀ 101 = 40 dB) 2 mV ripple × 101 ≈ 0.2 V at the output offset: MCP6002 V_os ≤ ±4.5 mV → output rests at 1.65 ± 0.45 V
U2A output (pin 1) back on the full 0–3.3 V scale. The beat is now a clear wave about 0.2 V tall. (Illustrative.)

Why the offset doesn't matterThe op-amp's own small input error also gets multiplied by 101, so the resting level can sit anywhere from about 1.2 to 2.1 V. The firmware tracks the baseline instead of assuming exactly 1.65 V, so this is fine.

If it's wrong: much more gain and noise plus offset push the output into a rail; much less and a beat is only a few ADC counts.

A5

Cut fast noise

C2 sits across R17. At slow frequencies a capacitor is an open circuit, so the gain is the full 101. At fast frequencies C2 lets current bypass R17, the feedback shrinks, and the gain falls toward 1. So this one capacitor turns the amplifier into a low-pass filter as well.

  • Sets where the gain starts to fall.
  • Shares the job: the corner depends on R17 × C2.
f_LP = 1 / (2π · R17 · C2) = 1 / (2π · 100 kΩ · 470 nF) = 3.4 Hz ≈ 203 bpm pass band 0.16–3.4 Hz ≈ 10–200 bpm gain at 1 Hz ≈ 97 · at 10 Hz ≈ 33 · at 50 Hz mains ≈ 7.8
Zoomed U2A output. Solid: with C2. Dashed: what it would look like without C2, with the fast noise amplified ×101 too. (Illustrative.)

Why we need itLight flicker, vibration, mains hum and radio pickup are all faster than any snail heart. Removing them before the ADC means less to clean up in software, and nothing fast enough to alias when sampling at 50 Hz.

Good to know: a non-inverting stage never has gain below 1, so very fast noise still passes at ×1. That's what R3 and C3 are for.

A6

Hand the signal to the ADC cleanly

The amplifier output passes through R3 to the net HB_ADC, which leaves on J6 pin 1 and reaches the STM32's pin PB0, an analog input.

  • Forms a last low-pass filter with C3, and limits current into the STM32 pin if anything ever goes wrong.
  • A charge reservoir. Each time the ADC samples, its tiny internal capacitor (a few pF) grabs a little charge. C3 is thousands of times bigger, so the voltage barely dips and the reading stays accurate.
f_c = 1 / (2π · 1 kΩ · 100 nF) = 1.6 kHz 12-bit ADC: 1 count = 3.3 V / 4096 = 0.81 mV at PB0 referred to SENSE (÷101): ≈ 8 µV per count
What the STM32 reads on PB0, in ADC counts (0–4095). Each beat is a few hundred counts tall around ~2048. (Illustrative.)
A7

Firmware turns the wave into beats per minute

This step isn't on the schematic; it runs on the flight controller's STM32. It's the last stage of the same chain, so it belongs here.

sample PB0 at 50 Hz (20 samples per beat even at 150 bpm) smooth (80 ms average) − baseline (6 s average) = beat signal envelope = recent peak size beat = signal rises above 40 % of envelope; re-arm below 10 % (hysteresis) ignore anything sooner than max(400 ms, 0.4 × usual interval) bpm = 60 000 / median(last 5 intervals in ms) quality = 100 · (1 − 2 · CV) (CV = spread ÷ mean of the intervals)

Why it's built this wayThe baseline subtraction undoes the offset from A4. The two thresholds stop noise from counting one beat twice. A median ignores one bad interval where an average would not. Every 2 s a SNAIL packet goes out over LoRa with the rate, quality and 20 waveform samples so the ground can see the raw shape too.

B

1.65 V reference and op-amp power

Block A needs a "middle" voltage to centre the heartbeat around. This block makes it: exactly half of 3.3 V, quiet and stiff, on the net VREF. It also holds the op-amp's power pins and their decoupling capacitor.

B1

Split 3.3 V in half

Two equal resistors in series between +3.3 V and ground form a voltage divider. The point between them sits at exactly half.

  • Top half, from +3.3 V.
  • Bottom half, to ground.
VREF = 3.3 V × R7 / (R6 + R7) = 3.3 × 10k / 20k = 1.65 V divider current = 3.3 V / 20 kΩ = 165 µA

Why the middleThe ADC reads 0–3.3 V. A signal centred at 1.65 V has the most room to swing both up and down before it clips.

B2

Smooth it

Any ripple on the 3.3 V rail would also appear, halved, on the divider. C4 filters it so the voltage the whole amplifier is referenced to stays steady.

  • Electrolytic, so it has a + side: + goes to the divider node, − to ground.
the divider looks like R6 ∥ R7 = 5 kΩ driving C4 f_c = 1 / (2π · 5 kΩ · 10 µF) = 3.2 Hz
B3

Make it stiff with a buffer

U2B's output (pin 7) is wired straight back to its − input (pin 6). That's a unity-gain buffer, or voltage follower: the output copies the + input exactly, but can supply current without the input noticing.

  • Second half of the same op-amp chip. Its output is the VREF net used by R15 and R16 in block A.
V_out = V_in = 1.65 V

Why not use the divider directlyR15 and R16 draw small, changing currents from VREF. A divider has 5 kΩ of internal resistance, so those currents would make VREF wobble, and the wobble would show up in the heartbeat signal. The op-amp output holds 1.65 V no matter what.

B4

Power the op-amp

U2C isn't a third amplifier. KiCad draws the power pins of a multi-unit chip as their own unit so the amplifier symbols stay clean.

  • Pin 8 (V+) to +3.3 V, pin 4 (V−) to ground.
  • Decoupling capacitor, placed right at pins 8 and 4. It supplies the chip's quick current spikes locally so the wires to the flight controller don't have to, and the chip sees a clean supply.

Ratiometric designVREF and the STM32's ADC both come from the same 3.3 V. If that rail drifts by 1 %, VREF and the ADC's full scale both drift by 1 %, so the reading in counts stays the same. That's why VREF is made from 3.3 V instead of a separate reference chip.

C

Connectors

Everything that enters or leaves the board goes through a connector: power in from the flight controller, the heartbeat and the I²C bus out to it, and cables to the sensor and three modules. The footprints are 2.5 mm JST-XH.

Power in: J5 and C10

The board makes no power of its own. The flight controller supplies both rails.

PinNetFeeds
1+5VIR LED through R1
2+3V3op-amp, phototransistor, divider, all three I²C modules, and (added 29 Oct) the DHT-11 and the MQ-7 heater
3GNDthe only ground return for the whole board
  • Power from the FC. The small diamond symbols next to it are PWR_FLAGs: they aren't parts, they just tell KiCad's electrical rule check that these nets are powered from outside the board.
  • Bulk capacitor on +3.3 V. It covers slower load changes (like the MAX30100's pulsed LEDs) that the small 100 nF capacitors can't.
load: +3.3 V < 25 mA · +5 V ≈ 17 mA (the IR LED) + the MQ-7 and DHT-11 (since 30 Oct) MQ-7 heater ≈ 33 Ω: 5 V / 33 Ω ≈ 150 mA (0.76 W) → +5 V total ≈ 170 mA FC payload channels allow 3 A each → we use about 4 %

Added 29 Oct: DHT-11 and MQ-7 on J6 pins 2 and 3

Rev C freed PB1 and PC6 when the heater was dropped. The two new modules use them. Since 30 Oct both run from +5V and GND on the board, and each sends one signal wire to the flight controller.

Module pinGoes toFC pinNotes
DHT-11 VCC (+)+5V+5V_ISDHT-11 works from 3.3 to 5.5 V; 5 V gives it more margin on long wires
DHT-11 GND (−)GNDGND
DHT-11 DATA (S / OUT)DHT_DATA → J6.3PC6needs a 4.7–10 kΩ pull-up to its VCC (5 V). 3-pin modules have one; a bare 4-pin sensor doesn't (pin 3 of a bare one is NC). PC6 is 5 V-tolerant as a digital input, so DATA at 5 V is safe; the firmware keeps the STM32's own 3.3 V pull-up off
MQ-7 VCC+5V+5V_ISfeeds its heater: ≈ 150 mA
MQ-7 GNDGNDGND
MQ-7 AOMQ7_AO → 10 kΩ → J6.2, 20 kΩ to GNDPB1analog, 0–5 V at the module, 0–3.33 V at PB1 after the divider

MQ-7 on 5 V: heater power = 5² / 33 Ω ≈ 0.76 W (its rated power) → the datasheet ppm curve applies after warm-up divider: V(PB1) = V(AO) × 20 kΩ / (10 kΩ + 20 kΩ) → 5 V at AO = 3.33 V at PB1; the firmware multiplies by 1.5

Why the divider is not optionalOn 5 V the MQ-7's AO can reach 5 V, and PB1 is not 5 V-tolerant in analog mode: without the divider a strong gas reading can damage the flight controller. Check it with the module powered: PB1 to GND must always read below 3.3 V. The divider values are in config.h (MQ7_DIV_TOP_OHM, MQ7_DIV_BOT_OHM) and at the top of SensorTest.

The sensor cable: J1

Four wires run from the board to the TCRT5000 on the shell. On the schematic they connect to block A only by label names.

  • The sensor it reaches, drawn in block A.

Sensors on one I²C bus: J7, J8, J9

I²C needs only two wires for any number of chips: SCL (clock, driven by the STM32) and SDA (data, both ways). Every chip has its own address and only answers when it hears it, so all the modules share the same SCL and SDA nets.

RefModuleAddressMeasures
J7SHT21 (GY-21): removed 30 Oct—not used since fw 1.5; box temperature comes from the BMP280, humidity from the DHT-11
J8BMP2800x76box pressure (300–1100 hPa, so it only works inside the sealed box)
J9MAX301000x57snail 2's pulse sensor (since 30 Oct): its own LEDs, photodiode and ADC, glued to the second snail's shell
  • Pins: 1 +3V3, 2 GND, 3 SCL, 4 SDA.
  • Same four, plus pin 5, which goes to the BMP280's SDO pin. SDO picks the address: SDO low = 0x76, SDO high = 0x77. J8 pin 5 is GND, so this module answers at 0x76.
  • Pins: 1 +3V3, 2 GND, 3 SCL, 4 SDA.

Where are the pull-up resistors?I²C lines are open-drain: chips can only pull them low, so something must pull them high. There are no pull-ups on this board; the sensor modules carry their own, and they end up in parallel on the bus.

Things to check before flight

From reading the current file against the firmware and the parts you're using. None is a wiring error in the schematic; they're places where the real hardware can differ from what the drawing implies.

  1. Wire the TCRT5000 by function, not by U1's pin numbers

    U1 uses KiCad's CNY70 symbol (there's no TCRT5000 in that library), so its pin numbers 1–4 are the CNY70's. Use the J1 table above and the A/K/C/E markings in the TCRT5000 datasheet when you solder the cable.

  2. J8 pin 5 must reach SDO, not CSB

    Many BMP280 modules also have a CSB pin. If CSB is pulled low at power-up the chip switches to SPI and disappears from the I²C bus. Leave CSB high or unconnected (most modules pull it up). J8's module has SDO → GND (0x76). If the scan shows 0x77 instead, its SDO is on the wrong rail.

  3. MAX30100 pull-ups

    Many purple GY-MAX30100 boards pull SDA/SCL up to 1.8 V. Your firmware already notes this. If the I²C scan shows 0x76 but not 0x57, that's the likely cause.

  4. Flash firmware 1.5 or newer, not the old binaries

    firmware/SnailPulse_Flight 1.3 (30 Oct) has the heater code switched off, measures two snails (TCRT5000 on PB0, MAX30100 on I²C), reads the DHT-11 on PC6, the MQ-7 on PB1 and the BMP280 (0x76). Older builds (1.0, 1.1) don't know about the new sensors, and the heater-on one drives PC6 as a PWM output, which fights the DHT-11. After flashing, the STATUS packet on the ground station must say fw 1.5, and the ENV sensor bits should read 0x76 (BMP280, MAX30100, SD, DHT-11 and MQ-7 all OK; bit 0 is the removed SHT21, bit 3 the heater NTC and bit 7 the dropped second BMP280).

  5. MQ-7 needs warm-up and its own airflow

    Its heater needs about 3 minutes after power-up before the reading settles, and a new sensor drifts for much longer. The can gets warm, so keep it away from the snail and from the BMP280 and DHT-11, or it will raise their readings.

Bring-up order

1. Power it: U2 pin 7 (VREF) should read 1.65 V 2. Finger on the TCRT5000: a ~1 Hz wave on HB_ADC 3. Turn RV3 so SENSE sits near 1 V DC 4. Flash firmware/tools/SensorTest/SensorTest.ino to the FLIGHT CONTROLLER (Generic STM32H7 · STM32H750VBTx · STM32CubeProgrammer SWD · ST-Link on PROG · BOOT0 = 0) 5. Serial Monitor on the FC's USB-C, 115200: I²C4 shows 0x57, 0x76; DHT-11 (PC6), MQ-7 (PB1), snail 1 (TCRT5000, PB0) and snail 2 (MAX30100) all say PASS

Nothing is uploaded to the SnailPulse board: it has no processor. The communication board and the power board keep the organizers' firmware.
